title: Unit 1b - From Java/Python to C++ (2)
summary: Title slide for Unit 1b covering C++ Basics 2, transitioning from Java/Python to C++. Authored by Mark Redekopp for CS 103.
main_text: This is the title slide for Unit 1b of CS 103, titled 'From Java/Python to C++ (2)'. The lecture is authored by Mark Redekopp and covers the second part of C++ basics, building on prior programming knowledge in Java or Python. The unit addresses arrays, functions, control structures, and loops in C++.
notes_text: This unit assumes students have prior programming experience in Java or Python and focuses on translating that knowledge into C++ syntax and idioms.

title: Pre-requisites for C++ Basics 2
summary: Lists prior knowledge students should have before this unit: if statements, for/while loops, arrays/lists, and functions from prior coursework.
main_text: In prior programming coursework, you should understand basic operation of: if statements, for and while loops (in Java or C++); the concept of an array or list storing multiple data items; breaking code into functions and their sequence of execution when they are called. These pre-requisites ensure students can follow the C++ syntax and semantics covered in this unit.
notes_text: Students are expected to have completed an introductory programming course. This unit bridges the gap between those languages and C++ by showing equivalent constructs and highlighting key differences.

title: Array Basics - Section Header
summary: Section divider slide introducing the Array Basics module of the lecture.
main_text: This is a section header slide introducing the Array Basics portion of the lecture. The following slides will cover what arrays are, how to declare and use them in C/C++, and how they differ from arrays and lists in Java and Python.
notes_text: Arrays are a fundamental data structure in C/C++ and understanding their fixed-size, contiguous-memory nature is critical for the rest of the course.

title: Motivating Example for Arrays
summary: Demonstrates why arrays are needed by showing the impracticality of using individual variables to store many student grades.
main_text: Suppose you need to store the grades for all students so you can compute statistics, sort them, print them, etc. You would need to store them in variables that you could access and use. This is easy if you have 3 or 4 students, but painful if you have many students. Enter arrays: a collection of many variables referenced by one name, where individual elements can be accessed with an integer index. The slide shows two code examples: one using three separate variables (int score1, score2, score3) which is manageable, and another attempting to declare 140 individual variables (score1 through score140) which is clearly impractical. Arrays solve this problem by letting you use a single name with an index to access any element.
notes_text: This motivating example is key to understanding why arrays exist. Without arrays, any program that processes collections of data would require an unwieldy number of individual variable declarations, making the code unmaintainable and inflexible.

images.description: Two code boxes comparing individual variable declarations (manageable for 3, impractical for 140) to motivate the need for arrays

title: Array Basics - Definition and Properties
summary: Defines arrays as fixed-size, named, ordered collections of same-type variables accessed by index and stored contiguously in memory.
main_text: An array is a fixed size, named collection of ordered variables of the same type that are accessed with an index and stored contiguously in memory. Key properties: Fixed size means arrays cannot grow or shrink after declaration. Named collection means one name refers to all variables in the array. Ordered/Accessed with an index means individual elements are accessed with their position/index using [] brackets. Same Type means all variables in one array must be the same type (one array cannot store both doubles and ints). Example code declares int scores[250] which allocates 250 integers with garbage values, then uses a for loop to read values: for(int i=0; i < 250; i++) { cin >> scores[i]; }. A memory diagram shows addresses 520, 524, 528, etc. with indices [0], [1], [2] through [249] storing values like 96, 84, 93, ..., 90.
notes_text: The contiguous memory layout is important for performance. Each element occupies the same amount of memory (e.g., 4 bytes for int), so the address of any element can be calculated as: base_address + index * sizeof(element).

images.description: Memory diagram showing array 'scores' stored contiguously with addresses 520-1516 and indices [0]-[249], demonstrating how array elements map to memory locations

title: An Analogy: Dorm/Apartment Buildings
summary: Uses a dormitory analogy to explain arrays: one building name with numbered rooms, like one array name with numbered indices.
main_text: Just as a dormitory is known by one name ('McCarthy') but has many dorm rooms, each with a number to identify them ('McCarthy 234')... arrays have one name for the whole collection of variables and use integer indexes to specify a particular element (e.g. McCarthy[234]). But you can still only access one at a time! A memory diagram shows the scores array with addresses 520, 524, 528, ..., 1076, indices [0], [1], [2], ..., [139], and values 96, 84, 93, ..., 90.
notes_text: This analogy helps students grasp the concept that an array name refers to a collection, while the index identifies a specific element within that collection, just like a room number within a building.

images.description: Photo of a USC dormitory building (McCarthy) used as an analogy for array naming and indexing

title: Array Intro (1) - Declaration and Initialization
summary: Shows C++ code demonstrating array declaration with fixed size, initialization with values, and behavior when fewer initializers are provided.
main_text: The code demonstrates three array scenarios: First, int data1[5] is declared with no initialization, so it contains garbage values. Second, int data2[] = {103, 104, 170, 201, 270} uses an initialization list and the compiler infers the size as 5. Third, int data3[5] = {103, 104, 105} provides fewer values than the array size, and remaining elements are filled with 0. Each case uses a for loop to print the values: for(int i=0; i < 5; i++) { cout << data[i] << " "; }. The code includes headers #include <iostream>, #include <algorithm>, #include <cmath> and uses namespace std.
notes_text: Key takeaway: uninitialized arrays contain garbage values, which is a common source of bugs. When an initialization list provides fewer values than the declared size, the remaining elements are zero-initialized. This is a C/C++ specific behavior that differs from Java where arrays are always zero-initialized.

title: Array Intro (2) - Out of Bounds Access and Variable-Length Arrays
summary: Demonstrates out-of-bounds array access dangers and shows that variable-length arrays using runtime values are problematic in C/C++.
main_text: The code demonstrates dangerous out-of-bounds access: accessing data2[5] (the 5th element of a 5-element array, which only has indices 0-4), data2[-2] (negative index), and data2[1000000] (far out of bounds). These accesses do not produce compile errors but lead to undefined behavior at runtime. The second part shows a commented-out attempt to declare a variable-length array: int n; cin >> n; int data4[n]; This is problematic because n is not known at compile time. While some compilers allow this as an extension, it is not standard C++ and can cause issues. The code then uses a loop to fill and print the variable-length array.
notes_text: C/C++ does not perform bounds checking on array accesses, unlike Java which throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. This makes C++ faster but more dangerous. Out-of-bounds access can corrupt other data, cause crashes (segmentation faults), or produce silent errors that are very hard to debug.

title: Index vs. Value
summary: Explains the distinction between an array index (position) and the value stored at that index, showing that indices can be any expression.
main_text: The expression in the square brackets is an index. Using array[index] yields the data/value in the array at that index. An index can be ANY EXPRESSION, even the value from an array or the return value from a function. For an array declared to be size n, only indices 0 to n-1 are legal. Example with scores array containing values {9, 0, 7, 8, 6}: int i = 1; int x = scores[2*i + 1] yields x=8 (index 3); int y = scores[scores[1]] yields y=9 (scores[1]=0, so scores[0]=9); int z = scores[max(4,2)] yields z=6 (max returns 4, scores[4]=6). The diagram labels 'scores[2*i+1]' with 'Value/data' pointing to the result and 'index' pointing to the expression inside brackets.
notes_text: Understanding the difference between an index and the value at that index is fundamental. Common beginner mistakes include confusing the position with the content. The ability to use any expression as an index is what makes arrays powerful when combined with loops.

images.description: Diagram showing scores[2*i+1] with labels indicating the bracket expression is the 'index' and the result is the 'Value/data', plus a memory table with addresses and values

title: Fixed (Statically) Sized Arrays
summary: Explains that C/C++ requires array sizes to be known at compile time, not runtime, and discusses stack overflow risks from variable-size allocations.
main_text: C/C++ needs to know the size of the array when the program is compiled (statically), not when it is run (dynamically). This implies the size of the array must be ONE, FIXED (or constant) size every time the program is run. Example of good: int data[42] where 42 is known at compile time. Example of bad: int n; cin >> n; int data[n] where n is not known at compile time. What could go wrong if we did allow variable-size array allocation? The analogy: Why don't hotels let you wait and specify how many rooms you want once you arrive? Too large an allocation can cause 'stack overflow' and corrupt the program. A memory layout diagram shows the program memory structure from address 0x00000000 to 0xffffffff with sections: Code, Global Data, Heap (growing up), and Stack (growing down from 0xc0000000).
notes_text: The stack has limited size (typically 1-8 MB). Arrays declared inside functions go on the stack. If a user enters a very large number for a variable-length array, it could overflow the stack. This is why C++ requires compile-time constant sizes for stack-allocated arrays.

images.description: Memory layout diagram showing program sections: Code at bottom (0x0), Global Data, Heap growing upward, and Stack growing downward from 0xc0000000, illustrating where arrays are allocated

title: Dealing With Variable Size Arrays
summary: Presents two approaches for handling unknown array sizes: allocating a large maximum-size array or using dynamic memory with the new operator.
main_text: C/C++ needs to know the size of the array when the program is compiled, not when it is run. Two approaches if we cannot know the necessary size at compile time: First approach: Allocate a LARGE array of the maximum size potentially needed and then use only a portion of it as the program runs. Example: int data[100]; int n; cin >> n; then use for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } to only use n elements. Second approach (Preferred): Use dynamic memory (i.e. the new operator) to allocate a variable size array. Example: int n; cin >> n; int* data = new int[n]; then use it similarly, followed by delete [] data for cleanup. This approach will be discussed in detail in a future unit. The note says: Major topic of discussion in a future unit (don't worry about it for now).
notes_text: For this course, the first approach (over-allocating) is commonly used. The second approach using dynamic memory (new/delete) is the professional solution but requires understanding pointers, which is covered later. Always track how many elements are actually used versus how many were allocated.

title: Coming From Other Languages - Array Comparison
summary: Compares C/C++ arrays with Java and Python arrays/lists, highlighting similarities (0-based indexing, loops) and key differences (fixed size, no bounds checking).
main_text: SIMILARITIES: Like Python and Java, C/C++ arrays use 0-based indexing (beginning element at index 0) and pair nicely with loops that can iterate over all elements of an array. DIFFERENCES: Unlike Python and Java, C/C++ arrays are fixed size (size must be a constant) and then cannot grow easily after that. They do not remember their size (no len() or .length) nor bounds-check an access, so accessing scores[1048726] will happily execute in C/C++ and likely cause a crash (aka the dreaded 'Segmentation Fault'). They are NOT objects (no .append() or .length) in C/C++, but degenerate to pointers (more to come soon). The slide shows equivalent code in Java (using Scanner and int[] scores = new int[150] with scores.length), Python (using scores = [0]*150 with len(scores)), and C++ (using int scores[150] with a hardcoded loop bound of 150).
notes_text: This comparison slide is critical for students transitioning from Java or Python. The lack of bounds checking in C/C++ is one of the most common sources of bugs and security vulnerabilities. Students must always be careful to track array sizes manually.

title: When Do We Need Arrays?
summary: Explains that arrays are needed when data must be revisited more than once; if only a single pass is needed, individual variables suffice.
main_text: Arrays can store many related data items of the same type. A better question is when do we need to store these related data items in an array? We need arrays when we need to revisit the data more than once. If we just want to find the min/max or average, we could just get the data from the user and update the sum or min/max as we go and not need to store each data item. Don't introduce arrays where they are not needed. Example 1 uses an array: read all 100 scores into scores[100], then iterate again to sum them. Example 2 avoids the array: use int val, sum = 0, read each value into val and add to sum in the same loop. Both compute the average, but the second approach uses only two variables instead of 100. The memory diagram contrasts the array approach (many memory slots) with the simpler approach (just sum and val).
notes_text: This is an important design principle. Using arrays when they are not needed wastes memory and adds complexity. Students should ask: 'Do I need to see this data again after processing it?' If yes, use an array. If no, a single variable is sufficient.

images.description: Memory diagram comparing array storage (scores with 150 slots) versus simple variables (sum and val) for computing an average

title: Function Basics - Section Header
summary: Section divider slide introducing the Function Basics module of the lecture.
main_text: This is a section header slide introducing the Function Basics portion of the lecture. The following slides will cover function signatures, prototypes, definitions, calling conventions, overloading, and related concepts in C++.
notes_text: Functions are the primary mechanism for code organization and reuse in C/C++. Understanding how to declare, define, and call functions is essential for writing maintainable programs.

title: Functions Overview - Decomposition and Abstraction
summary: Introduces functions as the unit of code decomposition and abstraction, using a Map Service example to illustrate breaking programs into smaller units.
main_text: Functions (aka procedures, procedures, or methods) are the unit of code decomposition and abstraction. Decomposition means breaking programs into smaller units of code. Abstraction means generalizing an action or concept without specifying how the details are implemented. A Map Service example shows function decomposition: ValidateInputs(), RetrieveMap(), GetOverlayData(), Render(), Publish() - each function handles one responsibility. A map of Los Angeles with traffic overlay illustrates the end result of these functions working together.
notes_text: Decomposition and abstraction are fundamental software engineering principles. Functions allow you to write code once and call it many times, reduce complexity by hiding implementation details, and make programs easier to test and debug.

images.description: Diagram showing a Map Service decomposed into five sequential functions: ValidateInputs, RetrieveMap, GetOverlayData, Render, Publish, illustrating function decomposition
Map of Los Angeles showing traffic overlay as an example output of the Map Service functions

title: Function Signatures/Prototypes
summary: Explains function signatures including name, parameters, and return type, and introduces the concept of a function prototype.
main_text: Functions are also called procedures or methods. We think of a function as a blackbox (don't know how it does the task internally) where we can provide inputs and get back a value. A function has: a name, zero or more input parameters, and 0 or 1 return (output) values (we only specify the type). The signature (or prototype) of a function specifies these aspects so others know how to 'call' the function. Example: int max(int a, int b); is a function signature/prototype for a function named 'max' that takes two integer parameters and returns an integer. A blackbox diagram shows inputs 'a' and 'b' going into a box labeled 'max' with a triangle output, and a form-like interface showing 'Max' with fields a and b and a Submit button.
notes_text: The prototype tells the compiler what types to expect for parameters and what type the function returns. This allows the compiler to check that function calls are correct even before seeing the function's implementation.

images.description: Blackbox diagram showing function 'max' with two input triangles 'a' and 'b' and one output triangle, representing function inputs and output

title: User Defined Functions - Three Steps
summary: Describes the three steps to create user-defined functions in C++: declare (prototype), define (implementation), and call.
main_text: We can define our own functions in 3 steps. Step 1: 'Declare' your function by placing the prototype (signature) at the top of your code. Step 2: 'Define' the function (actual code implementation) anywhere (above or below main()) by placing the code in { }. Step 3: 'Call' the function from main() or another function passing in desired inputs and using the return value (output). Example code shows: int max(int a, int b); as the prototype at the top, then int main() with variables and a call to max, then the definition int max(int a, int b) { if(a > b) return a; else return b; }. The return statement immediately stops the function and returns the value.
notes_text: The three-step process (declare, define, call) is the standard workflow in C++. The prototype must appear before any call to the function. The definition can appear anywhere in the file, even after main(). This separation allows for flexible code organization.

title: Functions Intro - printName and factorial Examples
summary: Shows complete examples of void and int-returning functions: printName (void, takes string) and factorial (int, takes int), with prototypes and definitions.
main_text: The code demonstrates two functions with prototypes and definitions. void printName(string name) prints 'Hello, ' followed by the name, but returns early if the name is empty. int factorial(int n) computes n! using a for loop: if n >= 0 and n == 0, return 1; otherwise int f = 1; for(int i = 1; i <= n; i++) { f *= i; } return f;. If n is negative, it returns -1 as an error value. The main function calls printName('Tina') and cout << factorial(4). Note that you cannot have 2 return values from a single function (the commented-out getCirclePerimAndArea example shows this limitation).
notes_text: Key concepts demonstrated: void functions that perform an action without returning a value, early return for error handling, using -1 as a sentinel error value, and the limitation that C++ functions can only return a single value. Students will later learn techniques to work around the single-return limitation.

title: Overloading: A Function's Signature
summary: Explains function overloading in C++: functions are unique by name and parameter types, not by return type. Same-name functions with different parameters are 'overloaded'.
main_text: What makes up a function signature unique: the name, and the number and type of arguments. No two functions are allowed to have the same signature. The following 6 functions are unique and allowed to have different implementations: int f1(int), int f1(double), int f1(int, double), void f1(char), double f1(), int f1(int, char). Return type does not make a function unique: int f1() and double f1() are not unique and thus not allowable. Two functions with the same name are said to be 'overloaded'. Example: int max(int, int); and double max(double, double); are overloaded versions of max.
notes_text: Function overloading is a form of polymorphism in C++. The compiler determines which version to call based on the argument types at the call site. This is resolved at compile time (static dispatch). Java supports the same concept, but Python does not have traditional function overloading.

title: Calling a Function (1) - Argument Mapping
summary: Explains how to call a function by passing arguments in order, and common mistakes to avoid when calling functions.
main_text: We 'call' or 'invoke' the function by using its name and placing variables or constants that the current function has declared in the order that we want them to map to the parameter/argument list. First variable listed (x) will map to the first parameter (a) in the function's argument list, the second variable (y) to the second parameter (b), etc. The correct call is: mx = max(x, y);. Don'ts: Don't relist the return type in the call (mx = int max(x, y) is wrong). Don't relist the type of the arguments (mx = max(int x, int y) is wrong). Don't use variable names that don't exist in the current function (mx = max(a, b) is wrong if a and b aren't declared in main). Don't forget to save the returned value (max(x, y); without assignment loses the result).
notes_text: The argument mapping is positional, not by name. The names of the parameters in the function definition are independent from the names of the variables passed in the call. This is a common source of confusion for beginners.

title: Calling a Function (2) - Execution Flow
summary: Explains the execution flow when a function is called: control transfers to the function, executes its body, and returns to the caller.
main_text: When a function is called, execution jumps to the function body, executes the code there, and then returns to the calling location with the return value. The slide traces through a complete example showing: main() declares variables x, y, mx and reads them, then calls mx = max(x, y). Execution jumps to the max function where parameters a and b receive copies of x and y. The function compares a and b, returns the larger one, and execution resumes in main() where the returned value is assigned to mx. The key insight is that function parameters are copies of the arguments passed in.
notes_text: This pass-by-value behavior means the function works with copies of the original variables. Changes to parameters inside the function do not affect the original variables in the calling function. Pass-by-reference will be covered later.

title: Calling a Function (3) - Parameter Scope
summary: Demonstrates that function parameters and local variables are separate from the caller's variables and exist only within the function scope.
main_text: Function parameters and local variables have their own scope. Variables declared inside a function (including parameters) are separate from variables in the calling function, even if they share the same name. When max(x, y) is called from main, the values of x and y are copied into new variables a and b inside the max function. These are completely independent memory locations. When the function returns, a and b cease to exist. The calling function's variables x and y remain unchanged.
notes_text: Understanding scope is essential for avoiding bugs. A common mistake is thinking that modifying a parameter inside a function will change the original variable. This will be revisited when pass-by-reference is introduced.

title: void Functions
summary: Explains void functions that perform actions but return no value, and how to use the return statement to exit early from them.
main_text: A void function performs an action but does not return a value. The return type is specified as void. You can use 'return;' (with no value) to exit the function early, but it is not required at the end of the function. Example: void printGreeting(string name) { if(name == "") { return; } cout << "Hello, " << name << endl; } will skip printing if the name is empty. Void functions are called as standalone statements, not as part of an expression: printGreeting("Alice"); is correct, while int x = printGreeting("Alice"); is wrong since there is no return value to assign.
notes_text: Void functions are useful for operations that have side effects (like printing output or modifying global state) without producing a result that needs to be captured.

main_text: This slide indicates a timeout for in-class exercises. Students are expected to practice writing and calling functions based on the material covered so far in the lecture.

title: Loops and Arrays Practice
summary: Exercise slide where students practice using loops to iterate over arrays and process array data.
main_text: This slide provides exercises combining loops with arrays. Students practice common array operations such as iterating through elements, computing sums and averages, finding minimum and maximum values, and searching for specific elements. These exercises reinforce the connection between loop control variables and array indices.
notes_text: The combination of loops and arrays is one of the most fundamental patterns in programming. Mastering this pattern is essential for all subsequent topics in the course.

title: for Loop Basics and Syntax
summary: Reviews the for loop syntax in C++: initialization, condition, and update expressions, with execution flow explained.
main_text: The for loop in C++ has three parts in its parentheses: initialization (executed once before the loop starts), condition (checked before each iteration, loop continues while true), and update (executed after each iteration). Syntax: for(init; condition; update) { body }. Example: for(int i = 0; i < 10; i++) { cout << i << endl; } prints numbers 0 through 9. The initialization declares and initializes the loop variable, the condition checks if we should continue, the body executes the repeated task, and the update modifies the loop variable to eventually make the condition false.
notes_text: The for loop is the most common loop for iterating a known number of times, especially when paired with arrays. The loop variable i is conventionally used as an array index.

title: while Loop Basics and Syntax
summary: Reviews while loop syntax and compares it with for loops, explaining when each is more appropriate.
main_text: A while loop checks its condition before each iteration and executes the body only if the condition is true. Syntax: while(condition) { body }. The initialization must happen before the while loop, and the update must happen inside the body. Example: int i = 0; while(i < 10) { cout << i << endl; i++; }. While loops are preferred when the number of iterations is not known in advance, such as reading input until a sentinel value is entered. For loops are preferred when the number of iterations is known or follows a regular pattern.
notes_text: Both for and while loops are interchangeable in terms of capability, but choosing the right one makes code more readable. For loops are idiomatic for counting iterations, while loops for event-driven repetition.

title: do..while Loop
summary: Introduces the do..while loop which executes the body at least once before checking the condition.
main_text: The do..while loop is a variant of the while loop that checks the condition after executing the body, guaranteeing at least one execution. Syntax: do { body } while(condition);. Note the semicolon after the closing parenthesis. This is useful when you need to perform an action before you can check whether to repeat it, such as getting user input and then checking if it is valid. Example: do { cout << "Enter a positive number: "; cin >> n; } while(n <= 0); keeps asking until the user enters a positive number.
notes_text: The do..while loop is less common than for or while loops but is the natural choice when the loop body must execute at least once. A common use case is input validation.

title: Loop Patterns and Common Tasks
summary: Covers common loop patterns including accumulation, counting, searching, and input processing with examples.
main_text: Common loop patterns include: Accumulation (summing values), Counting (how many items meet a criterion), Searching (finding a specific value), and Input processing (reading until end of input or sentinel). Each pattern uses a loop variable and an accumulator or flag variable. Examples demonstrate computing a sum, counting even numbers, finding the index of a target value, and reading input until the user enters -1. These patterns form the building blocks for more complex algorithms.
notes_text: Recognizing these patterns helps students solve problems more efficiently. Most array-processing tasks can be decomposed into one or more of these fundamental patterns.

title: Timeout: In-Class Exercises (Loops)
summary: Pause slide for students to work on in-class exercises related to loops.
main_text: This slide indicates a timeout for in-class exercises on loops. Students are expected to practice writing various loop types and applying common loop patterns to solve problems.
notes_text: Practice with loops is essential. Students should try converting between for, while, and do..while loops to understand their equivalence and appropriate use cases.

title: break Statement
summary: Introduces the break statement which ends the current loop immediately, and shows two alternatives for stopping a loop on invalid input.
main_text: The break statement ends the current loop immediately and continues execution after its last statement. It only stops the INNER-MOST containing loop, not ALL nested loops. Consider two alternatives for stopping a loop if an invalid (negative) guess is entered. Left approach uses a boolean flag: bool done = false; while(done == false) { cout << "Enter guess: " << endl; cin >> guess; if(guess < 0) done = true; } else { // Process guess } }. Right approach uses break: bool done = false; while(true) { cout << "Enter guess: " << endl; cin >> guess; if(guess < 0) break; } // Process guess // If guess < 0 we would skip this }. Both approaches achieve the same result but the break version is often simpler.
notes_text: The break statement provides a clean way to exit a loop from the middle. The boolean flag approach is more traditional but can be more verbose. Note that break only exits the innermost loop in nested loop situations.

images.description: Two side-by-side code boxes comparing a boolean flag approach (left) and a break statement approach (right) for exiting a loop on invalid input

title: break Statement - Execution Flow
summary: Animated version of the break slide showing execution flow arrows to illustrate how the boolean flag and break approaches control loop execution.
main_text: This slide adds execution flow annotations to the break statement comparison. In the boolean flag approach (left), when guess < 0: (1) done is set to true, (2) the loop continues to the condition check at the top, (3) the condition done == false is now false so the loop exits. In the break approach (right), when guess < 0: (1) break immediately exits the loop body and jumps past the closing brace. The arrows show that the flag approach requires the loop to complete one more condition check, while break exits immediately. Both approaches skip the 'Process guess' code when the input is invalid.
notes_text: The flow arrows make the control flow difference clear. With the flag approach, control flows back to the while condition naturally. With break, control jumps directly out of the loop. Understanding this difference is important for writing correct loop logic.

images.description: Two code boxes with numbered flow arrows showing execution paths: left uses done=true flag with arrows looping back to condition, right uses break with arrow jumping out of loop

title: continue Statement
summary: Introduces the continue statement which skips the rest of the current iteration and starts the next, and shows an alternative using if conditions.
main_text: The continue statement starts the next iteration of the loop immediately by going to the update statement of a for loop or top of the while loop. Consider two alternatives for repeating a loop to get a new guess if an invalid (negative) guess is entered. Often continue can be eliminated by changing the if condition. Left approach uses continue: while(done == false) { cout << "Enter guess: " << endl; cin >> guess; if(guess < 0) { continue; } // Process guess (only here if guess >= 0) }. Right approach uses modified condition: while(done == false) { cout << "Enter guess: " << endl; cin >> guess; if(guess >= 0) { // Process Guess } }. The right approach inverts the condition and wraps the processing code, achieving the same effect without continue.
notes_text: The continue statement can often be replaced by restructuring the if-else logic. Many style guides recommend avoiding continue when the logic can be expressed more clearly with if conditions, as it can make code harder to follow.

images.description: Two side-by-side code boxes comparing continue approach (left) and inverted if-condition approach (right) for skipping invalid input processing

title: continue Statement - Execution Flow
summary: Animated version showing execution flow arrows for continue statement, illustrating how control jumps back to the loop top.
main_text: This slide adds execution flow annotations to the continue statement comparison. In the continue approach (left), when guess < 0, the continue statement causes execution to jump back to the top of the while loop, skipping the 'Process guess' code. The arrow shows control flowing from continue directly to the while condition check. In the inverted condition approach (right), when guess >= 0, the processing code executes normally (1), and then the loop continues to its next iteration (2). When guess < 0, the if condition is false, so the processing code is simply skipped.
notes_text: The flow arrows demonstrate that continue and a restructured if achieve the same result. The restructured version is generally preferred because it is easier to read and understand at a glance.

main_text: This is an in-class exercise slide titled 'Turn 360'. The starter code provides: #include <iostream>, #include <iomanip>, using namespace std; int main() { // Write your code here! return 0; }. Students are asked to write code to complete the exercise. A grid is shown on the right side with a blue square object and two circular arrows indicating counterclockwise and clockwise rotation.

title: Recall: Scope
summary: Reviews variable scope: lifetime and visibility determined by the curly braces {} where the variable is declared. Variables die at the end of their enclosing block.
main_text: Scope refers to the lifetime and visibility of a variable. Recall variables are just memory slots in the computer; eventually the program will reclaim those slots and the variables will 'die'. How long are those slots allocated and reserved for your use (i.e. what is their lifetime)? What parts of your program can access the variables? In C/C++, a variable's scope is the curly braces {} it is declared within. Main Point: A variable dies at the end of the {...} it was declared in. Example code: int main() { int i; cin >> i; if(i > 0) { int temp = 2*i; cout << temp << endl; } // temp died here. cout << temp << endl; // ERROR! f1(); return 0; } // i dies here. void f1() { // is i visible here? cout << i << endl; // No, this would be an error. }
notes_text: Scope is one of the most important concepts in C/C++. Variables declared inside a block (between { and }) are only accessible within that block. Accessing a variable outside its scope is a compile error. This applies to variables in if blocks, loops, and functions.

title: Declaring the Inductive Variable
summary: Explains that for-loop inductive variables declared in the initialization have scope limited to the loop, but can be reused in subsequent loops.
main_text: The initialization statement can be used to declare a control/inductive variable, but its scope is ONLY the for loop (even though it is not technically declared in the {..} of the for loop). Just realize that variable will die at the end of the loop. However, because it dies after the first loop you can use that same variable name in a subsequent loop. Example: int n; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cout << 3*i << endl; } // i dies here. cout << i << endl; // won't compile because i is dead. for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cout << 4*i << endl; } // reincarnated i dies again. return 0; } // n dies here.
notes_text: This is a subtle but important point about C++ scope rules. The for-loop variable declared in the init statement is scoped to the loop even though it appears outside the curly braces. This allows the clean pattern of reusing 'i' in multiple consecutive loops.

title: Single Statement Bodies
summary: Explains that single-statement if/else/loop bodies don't require curly braces, but recommends always using braces to prevent bugs.
main_text: The Rule: Place code for an if, else if, or else construct in curly braces { ... }. The Exception: An if or else construct with a single statement body does not require { ... }. Another if counts as a single statement. However, you should ALWAYS prefer { ... } even in single statement bodies so that editing later does not introduce bugs. Examples without braces: if (x == 5) y += 2; else y -= 3; cout << "done1" << endl; (the cout is NOT part of the else). while (x != 0) x--; cout << "done2" << endl; (the cout is NOT inside the while). for(int i=0; i < 10; i++) if(i % 2 == 0) cout << i << endl; cout << "done3" << endl; (the last cout is NOT inside the for loop).
notes_text: This is a best-practice recommendation. The Apple 'goto fail' SSL bug (2014) was caused by a missing brace around a single-statement body. Always using braces eliminates this entire class of bugs and makes code intent clearer.

title: Nested Loops Examples
summary: Demonstrates nested for loops where the inner loop completes all iterations for each iteration of the outer loop, with a tracing example.
main_text: Key idea: Perform all iterations of the inner loop before starting the next iteration of the outer loop. Said another way: The inner loop executes completely for each single iteration of the outer loop. Trace through the execution of this code and show what will be printed: int main() { for(int i=0; i < 2; i++) { for(int j=0; j < 3; j++) { cout << i << " " << j << endl; } } }. The trace shows: i=0,j=0 then i=0,j=1 then i=0,j=2 then i=0,j=3(exits inner) then i=1,j=0 then i=1,j=1 then i=1,j=2 then i=1,j=3(exits inner) then i=2(exits outer). Output pairs: 0 0, 0 1, 0 2, 1 0, 1 1, 1 2.
notes_text: Tracing nested loops is an essential skill. The total number of iterations is the product of the individual loop counts. Here: 2 * 3 = 6 iterations total. Nested loops are commonly used for 2D data processing like matrices.

title: Tips - Nested Loops and Multi-Dimensional Data
summary: Explains that nested loops naturally represent multi-dimensional data: 2 loops for 2D (rows/columns), 3 loops for 3D (rows/columns/planes).
main_text: Nested loops often help us represent and process multi-dimensional data. 2 loops allow us to process data that corresponds to 2 dimensions (i.e. rows/columns). 3 loops allow us to process data that corresponds to 3 dimensions (i.e. rows/columns/planes). A 2D grid is shown with row and column indices (0-4), with cell (2,3) highlighted. A 3D cube visualization shows many small cubes arranged in a cube shape, representing 3-dimensional data that would require 3 nested loops to process.
notes_text: This connection between nested loops and dimensions is fundamental to understanding algorithms for matrices, images, and other multi-dimensional data structures. Each loop level corresponds to one dimension of the data.

images.description: 2D grid with row/column indices 0-4, cell (2,3) highlighted, representing 2D data accessed with two nested loops
3D cube made of small metallic cubes representing 3-dimensional data requiring three nested loops

title: Understand Your Bodies - Loop Body Meaning
summary: Advises writing comments describing what each loop body represents abstractly, using a guessing game with nested loops as example.
main_text: When you write loops write a comment as to what the body of each loop means in an abstract sense. The body of the outer loop represents 1 game (and we repeat that over and over). The body of the inner loop represents 1 turn (and we repeat turn after turn). Example: int main() { int secret, guess; char again = 'y'; while(again == 'y') { // A single game. secret = rand() % 20; guess = -1; // inner loop. while(guess != secret) { // A turn of the game. cout << "Enter guess: "; cin >> guess; } cout << "Win!" << endl; cout << "Play again (y/n): "; cin >> again; } return 0; }. The outer while loop represents a complete game, the inner while loop represents individual turns within a game.
notes_text: Annotating loop bodies with their abstract meaning is a valuable debugging and documentation practice. It helps others (and your future self) understand the intent of the code without having to trace through every line.

title: Times Table - In-Class Exercise
summary: Exercise to print a 12x12 multiplication table using nested loops and iomanip for formatting.
main_text: This is an in-class exercise to generate a 12x12 multiplication times table. The starter code includes #include <iostream>, #include <iomanip>, using namespace std; and int main() with a comment to write code. The expected output is a formatted 12x12 grid where each cell (i,j) contains i*j, from 1*1=1 to 12*12=144. The table uses setw() from iomanip for proper column alignment. Students should use two nested for loops: the outer loop for rows (1-12) and the inner loop for columns (1-12), printing i*j with proper formatting.
notes_text: This exercise reinforces nested loops, I/O manipulators (setw for column width), and the connection between nested loops and 2D data. The times table is a classic beginner exercise.

title: The Loops That Keep On Giving - Infinite Loops (Bug Examples)
summary: Shows two examples of accidental infinite loops: one using assignment instead of comparison, and one missing the update statement.
main_text: There's a problem with the loops below. We all write 'infinite' loops at one time or another. Infinite loops never quit. When you do write such a program, just type 'Ctrl-C' at the terminal to halt the program. Left example: bool again = true; while(again = true) { ... if(val == -1) { again = false; } }. The bug is using = (assignment) instead of == (comparison) in the while condition, so again is always set to true. Right example: int i=0; while(i < 10) { cout << i << endl; i + 1; }. The bug is using i + 1 instead of i = i + 1 or i++, so i never changes and the loop runs forever.
notes_text: These are two of the most common causes of infinite loops. The assignment-vs-comparison bug (= vs ==) is especially tricky because it compiles without error. The missing update bug is easier to spot but still common among beginners.

title: The Loops That Keep On Giving - Bug Fixes Highlighted
summary: Shows the same infinite loop examples with the bugs highlighted and corrected: using == instead of =, and i = i + 1 instead of i + 1.
main_text: This slide highlights the fixes for the two infinite loop bugs. Left example fix: while(again == true) uses the equality comparison operator == instead of the assignment operator =. The highlighted correction shows 'again == true' in the while condition. Right example fix: i = i + 1; properly updates the loop variable instead of the expression i + 1 which computes but discards the result. The highlighted correction shows 'i = i + 1;' replacing the incorrect 'i + 1;'. Both fixes ensure the loops will eventually terminate.
notes_text: A useful defensive technique for the = vs == bug: put the constant on the left side of the comparison (e.g., while(true == again)). If you accidentally write = instead of ==, the compiler will catch it because you cannot assign to a constant.

title: Find the Unique Number (1) - Problem Introduction
summary: Introduces the problem of checking if all numbers in an array are unique, posing questions about the algorithmic approach.
main_text: Check if all the numbers in an array are unique. It may not be as easy even for a human when we increase the amount of numbers. Questions: What process would you use as a human? Can we do this in 1 pass? If we can only see 1 thing or perform 1 operation at a time, what other variables do we need? Do we always have to do the same amount of work, or might we find an answer 'early'? Sample data is shown: a large set of numbers from 1 to 98 arranged in rows, representing an array that students must check for uniqueness.
notes_text: This problem motivates the use of nested loops. Checking uniqueness requires comparing every element with every other element, which is an O(n^2) operation using nested loops. This is a classic introduction to algorithmic thinking.

title: Find the Unique Number (2) - First Element Comparisons
summary: Traces through comparing the first element (index 0) with all subsequent elements using the inner loop variable k.
main_text: Check if all numbers are unique. The trace shows an array with indices [0] through [6] and values starting with 5 at index 0. Using two variables J and K: J starts at 0 (the element we're comparing), and K iterates from 1 through 6 (the elements we compare against). Each step compares data[0] with data[k]: data[0]=5 vs data[1]=2, then data[0]=5 vs data[2]=8, then data[0]=5 vs data[3]=1, then data[0]=5 vs data[4]=7, then data[0]=5 vs data[5]=9, then data[0]=5 vs data[6]=3. After checking all, we've confirmed element 0 is unique among all elements. The question asks: 'We've seen all the numbers now? Can we state they are all unique? What are you remembering to answer that question? Can the computer do that?'
notes_text: This step-by-step trace helps students understand the inner loop of the nested loop approach. For just one element, we need n-1 comparisons. The key insight is that we need to remember whether any match was found, which requires a boolean variable.

images.description: Step-by-step trace showing array with 7 elements, J fixed at 0, K incrementing from 1 to 6, comparing data[0] against each subsequent element

title: Find the Unique Number (3) - Why Not Start k at 0
summary: Explains why the inner loop variable k should not start at the same index as j, since comparing an element with itself always yields a false match.
main_text: Why not start k at 0 as well? We never want to compare an element with itself. The diagram shows an array with index [0] containing value 5, with J=0 and K=0. A red prohibition symbol indicates that data[j] == data[k] when j and k are the same index would always be true, giving a false positive for a duplicate. The inner loop must skip the current element being checked by the outer loop.
notes_text: This is a subtle but critical point. If k starts at 0 when j is 0, data[0] == data[0] is always true, incorrectly indicating a duplicate. The solution is to start k at j+1 (or skip when k==j), which also avoids redundant comparisons.

images.description: Array diagram with prohibition symbol over the case where J=0 and K=0, showing that comparing an element with itself is invalid

title: Find the Unique Number (4) - Second Element Comparisons
summary: Traces through comparing the second element (index 1) with all subsequent elements, continuing the uniqueness check algorithm.
main_text: Check if all numbers are unique. The trace now shows J=1, comparing data[1] against subsequent elements. The array has value 2 at index 1. K iterates from 2 through 6: data[1]=2 vs data[2]=8, then data[1]=2 vs data[3]=1, then data[1]=2 vs data[4]=7, then data[1]=2 vs data[5]=9, then data[1]=2 vs data[6]=3. No match is found, so element 1 is also unique among subsequent elements. Note that we don't need to compare data[1] with data[0] because that comparison was already done when J was 0.
notes_text: By starting k at j+1 instead of 0, we avoid both self-comparison and redundant comparisons. Each pair is compared exactly once, reducing the total comparisons from n*n to n*(n-1)/2.

images.description: Step-by-step trace showing J=1, K incrementing from 2 to 6, comparing data[1] against each subsequent element

title: Computing e^x Using Taylor Series
summary: Demonstrates computing e^x using its Taylor series expansion with a for loop that incrementally builds the numerator and denominator.
main_text: The Taylor series for e^x is: e^x = 1 + x + x^2/2! + x^3/3! + x^4/4! + ... The code computes this: double x; cin >> x; double x_to_i = 1; int i_fact = 1; double e_x = 1; for(int i=1; i < 10; i++) { x_to_i *= x; i_fact *= i; e_x += x_to_i / i_fact; } cout << e_x << endl;. The key insight is that instead of recomputing x^i and i! from scratch each iteration, we maintain running products: x_to_i accumulates x^i by multiplying by x each step, and i_fact accumulates i! by multiplying by i each step. Examples shown: e^0.6, e^0.8, and e^2.2 with their expanded series.
notes_text: This is an excellent example of incremental computation within a loop. Rather than using pow() and a factorial function (which would be O(n) each), we compute each term in O(1) by building on the previous term. This pattern appears frequently in numerical computing.

images.description: Mathematical formula showing e^x Taylor series expansion and three specific examples with different x values
