The following slides provide a comprehensive review of conditional structures, iterative structures, and other control flow mechanisms in C++. These slides may repeat material from earlier in the lecture with additional detail or from a different perspective.
notes_text: The review section is designed for students to solidify their understanding. The slides that follow cover the same topics (conditionals, loops, break/continue) in a more detailed, standalone manner suitable for study and reference.

title: Module 4: Conditional Structures
summary: Section header for Module 4 covering conditional structures: comparison operators, logical operators, if statements, and switch statements.
main_text: This is a module header slide for Module 4: Conditional Structures. The module covers comparison operators, logical operators, if statements, and switch statements. These are the primary mechanisms for making decisions in C++ programs.
notes_text: Conditional structures allow programs to execute different code paths based on runtime conditions. This module reviews the operators and statements needed to express those conditions.

title: Comparison Operators
summary: Lists the six C/C++ comparison operators: ==, !=, <, >, <=, >= with their meanings and usage examples.
main_text: To perform comparison of variables, constants, or expressions in C/C++ we can use the basic 6 comparison operators. == means Equality, example: if(x == y). != means Inequality, example: if(x != 7). < means Less-than, example: if(x < 0). > means Greater-than, example: if(y > x). <= means Less-than OR equal to, example: if(x <= -3). >= means Greater-than OR equal to, example: if(y >= 2). Each operator compares two values and produces a boolean result (true or false).
notes_text: The most common mistake is using = (assignment) instead of == (comparison). Remember: single = assigns a value, double == compares values. All comparison operators return a boolean value that can be used in if statements, while loops, and other conditional contexts.

title: If...Else If...Else
summary: Explains the if/else if/else chain for handling more than two cases, with any number of else-if branches and an optional else.
main_text: Got more than 2 cases, use 'else if'. Can have any number of else if statements. else if is optional. Reminder: else is optional. { ... } indicate code associated with the if, else if, else block. Syntax: if (condition1) { // executed if condition1 is true } else if (condition2) { // executed if condition2 is true but condition1 was false } else if (condition3) { // executed if condition3 is true but condition1 and condition2 were false } else { // executed if neither condition above is true }. A train analogy shows if, else if, else if, else as connected train cars, where only one car's passengers (code block) are selected.
notes_text: The key point is that in an if/else-if chain, conditions are evaluated top-to-bottom, and only the FIRST true condition's block executes. All subsequent blocks are skipped. This is different from a series of independent if statements.

images.description: Train analogy showing if, else if, else if, else as connected train cars, illustrating that only one branch executes

title: Mutually Exclusive Conditions
summary: Contrasts if/else-if chains (mutually exclusive, only one branch executes) with independent if statements (multiple branches can execute).
main_text: What will each implementation print if 'grade' is 95? Left implementation uses if/else if chain: if(grade >= 90) prints 'A range', else if(grade >= 80) prints 'B range', else if(grade >= 70) prints 'C range', else if(grade >= 60) prints 'D range', else prints 'Not gonna happen!'. With grade=95, only 'A range' prints because the first condition is true and all subsequent else-if blocks are skipped. Right implementation uses independent if statements: if(grade >= 90) prints 'A range', if(grade >= 80) prints 'B range', if(grade >= 70) prints 'C range', if(grade >= 60) prints 'D range', else prints 'Not gonna happen!'. With grade=95, it prints 'A range', 'B range', 'C range', AND 'D range' because each if is evaluated independently.
notes_text: This is one of the most important distinctions in conditional logic. Using else-if ensures mutual exclusivity - exactly one branch executes. Using separate if statements allows multiple branches to execute. Choose the right structure based on whether your conditions are meant to be mutually exclusive.

title: If...Else If...Else - Guideline for Mutually Exclusive Code
summary: Guideline: use if/else-if/else for mutually exclusive code blocks instead of multiple independent if statements.
main_text: Guideline: If various blocks of code are mutually exclusive then put them in an if..else if..else structure and not many individual if..if..if.. statements. BAD example: if (x < 0) { cout << "negative" << endl; } if (x >= 0) { cout << "positive" << endl; }. These are mutually exclusive conditions (a number cannot be both negative and non-negative), so using separate if statements is wasteful and error-prone. GOOD example: if (x < 0) { cout << "negative" << endl; } else { cout << "positive" << endl; }. Using else ensures mutual exclusivity and is more efficient because the second condition is not evaluated when the first is true.
notes_text: Using else-if chains for mutually exclusive conditions is both more efficient (fewer condition evaluations) and less error-prone (impossible for multiple branches to execute). It also makes the code's intent clearer to other programmers.

title: Logical Operators
summary: Introduces the three logical operators in C/C++: && (AND), || (OR), and ! (NOT) for creating compound conditions.
main_text: We can create compound conditions by using the logical AND, OR, and NOT operators. && means AND, example: if((x==0) && (y==0)) - true only when both conditions are true. || means OR, example: if((x < 0) || (y < 0)) - true when at least one condition is true. ! means NOT, example: if(!x) - inverts the boolean value. These operators allow combining multiple simple comparisons into more complex conditions.
notes_text: Logical operators are essential for expressing complex conditions. Remember operator precedence: ! has highest precedence, then &&, then ||. When in doubt, use parentheses to make the intended evaluation order explicit.

title: Logical AND, OR, NOT - Truth Tables
summary: Shows complete truth tables for AND, OR, and NOT operations, explaining that AND requires all true, OR requires any true.
main_text: The following tables show how the logical operations are evaluated under any set of values. AND: All inputs must be true for the resulting expression to be true. If even one is false, the condition fails (false). Truth table: F&&F=F, F&&T=F, T&&F=F, T&&T=T. OR: If any input is true the condition evaluates to true. Truth table: F||F=F, F||T=T, T||F=T, T||T=T. NOT: Inverts the value. Truth table: !F=T, !T=F.
notes_text: Truth tables are the foundation for understanding logical operations. AND is like multiplication (any zero makes the product zero), OR is like addition (any non-zero makes the sum non-zero). These tables should be memorized.

images.description: Three truth tables showing all input/output combinations for AND, OR, and NOT logical operations

title: Exercise - Range Check Conditions
summary: Exercise asking which of four conditions correctly checks if integer x is in the range [-1 to 5].
main_text: Which of the following is NOT a condition to check if the integer x is in the range [-1 to 5]? a. x >= -1 && x <= 5 (correct - standard AND range check). b. -1 <= x <= 5 (INCORRECT - this is not valid C/C++ syntax; it chains comparisons which doesn't work as intended). c. !(x < -1 || x > 5) (correct - uses DeMorgan's: NOT outside range means inside range). d. x > -2 && x < 6 (correct - equivalent range for integers since x is an int). See solutions at end of slides.
notes_text: Option b is the answer - it is NOT a valid condition. In C/C++, -1 <= x <= 5 first evaluates -1 <= x (which is 0 or 1), then compares that result to 5, which is always true. This is a very common mistake for students coming from math notation.

title: Conditions and DeMorgan's Theorem
summary: Explains DeMorgan's theorem: two equivalent ways to express any logical condition by distributing NOT over AND/OR.
main_text: DeMorgan's theorem says there are always two ways to express a logic condition. Write a condition that eats a sandwich if it has neither tomato nor lettuce: if(!tomato && !lettuce) { eat_sandwich(); } is equivalent to if(!(tomato || lettuce)) { eat_sandwich(); }. DeMorgan's theorem: !a && !b is equivalent to !(a || b). !a || !b is equivalent to !(a && b). More details in EE 109 and CS 170.
notes_text: DeMorgan's theorem is fundamental to boolean algebra and appears throughout computer science. It allows you to rewrite conditions in whichever form is more readable. The theorem states that negation distributes over AND/OR by swapping the operator.

title: Timeout: In-Class Exercises (Conditionals)
summary: Pause slide for in-class exercises on conditional structures, listed as 'nth' exercise.
main_text: This slide indicates a timeout for in-class exercises on conditional structures. Students are expected to practice writing if/else if/else chains, using logical operators, and applying DeMorgan's theorem.
notes_text: Practice with conditional logic is essential for building correct programs. Students should pay special attention to mutually exclusive conditions and proper use of logical operators.

title: Common Mistakes 1 - Assignment vs Equality and if vs if-else
summary: Warns about using = instead of == in conditions, and using multiple independent if statements instead of if-else for mutually exclusive conditions.
main_text: Common Mistake 1: Using assignment operator (=) rather than equality check operator (==). If you accidentally use '=', it will convert the assigned value to a Boolean. Recall the computer uses 0 to mean false, non-zero to mean true. Wrong: if(x = 0) assigns 0 to x, evaluates to false. Right: if(x == 0) compares x to 0. Wrong: if(x != y) { x = 5; } if(x == y) { y = 7; } - these should be if/else since they are mutually exclusive. Right: if(x != y) { x = 5; } else { y = 7; }. Tip: When comparing with a constant, many companies and style guides recommend flipping the order: if(0 == x). This way, if you accidentally write if(0 = x), the code won't compile because you can't assign to a constant.
notes_text: The = vs == bug is one of the most common and dangerous C/C++ mistakes because the code compiles without error. The 'constant on left' technique (Yoda conditions) is a defensive programming practice used by many professional codebases.

title: Common Mistakes 2 - Chained Comparisons and OR Conditions
summary: Warns about invalid chained comparisons (0 <= x <= 9) and incorrect OR conditions (x == 0 || 1) in C/C++.
main_text: All conditions must be formulated as a combination of comparisons of two values at a time. Recall the computer uses 0 to mean false, non-zero to mean true. Wrong: if(0 <= x <= 9) - this chains comparisons which doesn't work as intended in C/C++. It first evaluates 0 <= x (yielding 0 or 1), then compares that result to 9, which is always true. Right: if((0 <= x) && (x <= 9)). Wrong: if(x == 0 || 1) - the || 1 is always true because 1 is non-zero (true). Right: if((x == 0) || (x == 1)). Each comparison must independently compare two values.
notes_text: These mistakes stem from trying to write conditions the way they appear in mathematical notation. C/C++ requires explicit, pairwise comparisons joined by logical operators. Both of these bugs compile without warnings and produce incorrect behavior at runtime.

title: Other Selection Structures
summary: Introduces switch statements and ternary operator as alternative selection structures to if-else in C/C++.
main_text: C/C++ (and some other languages) provide alternative structures to if..else: the switch (case) statement and the ternary operator (cond ? x : y). We will not require knowledge of these but simply recommend you briefly look over this material. Slides covering these structures are available at the end of the packet.
notes_text: While if/else is the primary conditional structure, switch statements are useful for selecting among many constant values, and the ternary operator provides concise inline conditional expressions. Both are common in professional C++ code.

title: Module 5: Iterative Structures
summary: Section header for Module 5 covering while, do..while, and for loops.
main_text: This is a module header slide for Module 5: Iterative Structures. The module covers while, do..while, and for Loops. These are the looping mechanisms available in C++ for repeating code execution.
notes_text: Iterative structures (loops) are essential for any non-trivial program. This module provides a comprehensive review of all three loop types in C++.

title: Motivation for Loops
summary: Motivates loop usage by contrasting writing 1000 individual cout statements versus a single for loop to print numbers 1-1000.
main_text: To reduce repetition, we can generalize our code to use a loop. Take a simple task such as outputting the first 1000 positive integers. We could write 1000 cout statements: cout << 1 << endl; cout << 2 << endl; cout << 3 << endl; // hundreds more cout statements... cout << 999 << endl; cout << 1000 << endl;. Yikes! We could do it, but it would be painful! Or we could use a loop: for(int i=1; i <= 1000; i+=1) { cout << i << endl; }. The loop version is concise, maintainable, and easily modified to print different ranges.
notes_text: This motivation makes the value of loops immediately clear. Any task that involves repetition with a pattern is a candidate for a loop. The loop variable captures the changing part of the repeated task.

title: 4 Necessary Parts of a Loop
summary: Identifies the four essential parts of any loop: initialization, condition, body, and update, with a flowchart showing their relationship.
main_text: Loops involve writing a task to be repeated. Regardless of that task, there must be 4 parts to make a loop work. Initialization: Initialization of the variable(s) that will control how many iterations (repetitions) the loop will execute. Condition: Condition to decide whether to repeat the task or stop the loop. Body: Code to repeat for each iteration. Update: Modify the variable(s) related to the condition (without the update, the condition could be TRUE forever leading to an 'infinite loop'). Example: for(int i=1; i <= 1000; i+=1) { cout << i << endl; }. The flowchart shows: Initialization (i=1) at top, then Condition (i <= 1000) diamond, if True goes to Body (cout << i), then Update Statement (i += 1), back to Condition. If False, goes to Code after the loop.
notes_text: Every loop, regardless of type (for, while, do-while), must have all four parts. Forgetting the update is the most common cause of infinite loops. The initialization and update together define the progression through the iterations.

images.description: Flowchart showing the four parts of a loop: Initialization leads to Condition diamond, True branch goes to Body then Update then back to Condition, False branch exits to Code after the loop

title: Types of Loops - for and while (do..while)
summary: Introduces the two main loop types in C++: for loops and while loops (with do..while as a variant), showing equivalent code.
main_text: There are 2 (and a half) kinds of loops: for loops and while (do..while) loops. For loop: int i; for(i = 1; i <= 1000; i++) { cout << i << endl; } // following statements. While loop equivalent: int i = 1; while(i <= 1000) { // repetitive task: cout << i << endl; i++; // update } // following statements. The 4 parts are listed: Initialization, Condition, Body, Update. There is a variant of the while loop which is the do..while loop which we'll cover later.
notes_text: For and while loops are functionally equivalent - any for loop can be rewritten as a while loop and vice versa. The for loop is more compact for counting iterations because it groups initialization, condition, and update in one line.

title: Nested Loops - Section Header
summary: Section divider introducing the Nested Loops portion of the review.
main_text: This is a section header slide introducing the Nested Loops section. The following slides provide detailed coverage of how nested loops work, including sequencing, examples, and practical applications.
notes_text: Nested loops are essential for processing multi-dimensional data and solving problems that require comparing all pairs of elements.

title: Nested Loop Sequencing
summary: Shows the execution sequence of nested while loops with numbered steps, demonstrating that the inner loop runs completely for each outer iteration.
main_text: Key Idea: The inner loop runs in its entirety for each iteration of the outer loop. The code shows: while(cond1) { // code1; while(cond2) { // code2 } // code3 }. Execution sequence with Cond1: T T F and Cond2 rows: T T F and T F. Steps numbered 1-16: (1) check cond1=T, (2) code1, (3) check cond2=T, (4) code2, (5) check cond2=T, (6) code2, (7) check cond2=F exit inner, (8) code3, (9) check cond1=T, (10) code1, (11) check cond2=T, (12) code2, (13) check cond2=F exit inner, (14) code3, (15) check cond1=F exit outer, (16) following statements. A flowchart shows the nested structure with cond1 as outer decision and cond2 as inner decision.
notes_text: Understanding the exact sequencing of nested loops is critical for debugging. The inner loop's condition is re-initialized each time the outer loop iterates. Trace through carefully to verify loop behavior.

images.description: Flowchart showing nested while loop structure with cond1 as outer decision and cond2 as inner decision, with True/False branches and code blocks

title: Nested Loops Example 1 - Guessing Game
summary: Review of the guessing game example with nested loops: outer loop for games, inner loop for turns within each game.
main_text: When you write loops consider what the body of each loop means in an abstract sense. The body of the outer loop represents 1 game (and we repeat that over and over). The body of the inner loop represents 1 turn (and we repeat turn after turn). Code: int main() { int secret, guess; char again = 'y'; // outer loop. while(again == 'y') { // Choose secret num. 0-19. secret = rand() % 20; guess = -1; // inner loop. while(guess != secret) { cout << "Enter guess: "; cin >> guess; } cout << "Win!" << endl; cout << "Play again (y/n): "; cin >> again; } return 0; }. Brackets show '1 game' spanning the outer body and '1 turn' spanning the inner body.
notes_text: This is a duplicate of slide 41 in the review section. The key takeaway is annotating loop bodies with their abstract meaning. The outer while controls game repetition, the inner while controls turn repetition within a game.

title: Nested Loops Example 2 - Tracing i and j
summary: Review of nested for loop tracing example showing output pairs (i,j) for i in [0,2) and j in [0,3).
main_text: Key idea: Perform all iterations of the inner loop before starting the next iteration of the outer loop. Said another way: The inner loop executes completely for each single iteration of the outer loop. Trace through the execution of this code and show what will be printed: int main() { for(int i=0; i < 2; i++) { for(int j=0; j < 3; j++) { cout << i << " " << j << endl; } } }. The trace table shows: i=0,j=0; i=0,j=1; i=0,j=2; i=0,j=3(exits); i=1,j=0; i=1,j=1; i=1,j=2; i=1,j=3(exits). The highlighted cout line shows the output statement.
notes_text: This is a duplicate of slide 39. Tracing through nested loops step by step is essential practice. Note how j resets to 0 each time the outer loop's body re-executes.

title: Tips - Nested Loops and Multi-Dimensional Data (Review)
summary: Review slide repeating that 2 nested loops process 2D data and 3 nested loops process 3D data.
main_text: Nested loops often help us represent and process multi-dimensional data. 2 loops allow us to process data that corresponds to 2 dimensions (i.e. rows/columns). 3 loops allow us to process data that corresponds to 3 dimensions (i.e. rows/columns/planes). A 2D grid with indices and a 3D cube visualization are shown as before.
notes_text: This is a duplicate of slide 40 in the review section. The relationship between loop nesting depth and data dimensions is a key conceptual framework.

images.description: 2D grid and 3D cube illustrating the correspondence between nested loop depth and data dimensions

title: I/O Manipulators
summary: Covers cout manipulators: setw for column width, setprecision for decimal digits, fixed for fixed-point, and boolalpha for boolean output.
main_text: Manipulators control HOW cout handles certain output options and how cin interprets the input data (but print nothing themselves). Must #include <iomanip>. Common examples: setw(n) separates consecutive outputs by n spaces. setprecision(n) uses n digits to display doubles (both the integral and decimal parts). fixed uses the precision for only the digits after the decimal point. boolalpha shows Booleans as true and false rather than 1 and 0. Separated by << or >> and used inline with actual data. Other than setw, manipulators continue to apply to other output until changed. Example: double pi = 3.14159; cout << pi << endl; prints 3.14159. cout << setprecision(2) << fixed << pi << endl; prints 3.14. Reference: http://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/io/manip.
notes_text: setw is unique among manipulators because it only affects the next output operation. All other manipulators (setprecision, fixed, boolalpha) are 'sticky' and persist until explicitly changed. This distinction is important for formatting tables.

title: break Statement (Review)
summary: Review of the break statement showing boolean flag vs break approaches for exiting a loop, with execution flow arrows.
main_text: break ends the current loop immediately and continues execution after its last statement. Only stops the INNER-MOST containing loop, not ALL nested loops. Two alternatives for stopping a loop if an invalid (negative) guess is entered are shown with flow arrows. The boolean flag approach (left) sets done = true and continues to the condition check. The break approach (right) immediately exits the loop body.
notes_text: This is a review duplicate of slides 31-32. The break statement is a cleaner alternative to boolean flags when you need to exit a loop from the middle.

title: continue Statement (Review)
summary: Review of the continue statement showing continue vs inverted if-condition approaches for skipping invalid input.
main_text: continue starts the next iteration of the loop immediately by going to the update statement of a for loop or top of the while loop. Two alternatives shown: using continue to skip processing on invalid input, and using an inverted if condition to wrap the processing code. Often continue can be eliminated by changing the if condition. The flow arrows show continue jumping to the top of the while loop.
notes_text: This is a review duplicate of slides 33-34. The inverted condition approach is generally preferred for readability.

title: Odds and Ends Regarding C/C++ Loops - Section Header
summary: Section divider for miscellaneous loop-related topics in C/C++.
main_text: This is a section header slide introducing the Odds and Ends section regarding C/C++ loops. The following slides cover additional loop-related topics including scope, inductive variables, single statement bodies, and infinite loops.
notes_text: These topics cover important practical details that students need to know for writing correct C++ loop code.

title: Recall: Scope (Review)
summary: Review of variable scope concepts: variables die at the end of the curly braces they were declared in.
main_text: Scope refers to the lifetime and visibility of a variable. Recall variables are just memory slots in the computer; eventually the program will reclaim those slots and the variables will 'die'. In C/C++, a variable's scope is the curly braces {} it is declared within. Main Point: A variable dies at the end of the {...} it was declared in. The same code example from slide 36 is shown: temp declared inside an if block dies when the if block ends, attempting to use it outside produces an error. Function f1() cannot access variable i from main().
notes_text: This is a review duplicate of slide 36. Scope is fundamental to understanding variable lifetime and visibility in C/C++.

title: Declaring the Inductive Variable (Review)
summary: Review of for-loop variable scope: the inductive variable declared in the for-init dies at loop end but can be reused in subsequent loops.
main_text: The initialization statement can be used to declare a control/inductive variable, but its scope is ONLY the for loop (even though it is not technically declared in the {..} of the for loop). Just realize that variable will die at the end of the loop. However, because it dies after the first loop you can use that same variable name in a subsequent loop. Same example as slide 37: for(int i=0; i < n; i++) declares i scoped to the loop. After the loop, i is dead. A second for(int i=0; i < n; i++) can reuse the name.
notes_text: This is a review duplicate of slide 37. The for-loop variable scope rule is a C++ specific behavior that is important for writing clean loop code.

title: The Loops That Keep On Giving - Infinite Loops (Review, Bug Examples)
summary: Review of infinite loop bugs: assignment in condition (again = true) and missing update (i + 1 instead of i = i + 1).
main_text: There's a problem with the loops below. We all write 'infinite' loops at one time or another. Infinite loops never quit. When you do write such a program, just type 'Ctrl-C' at the terminal to halt the program. Same two examples as slides 43-44: left uses while(again = true) instead of while(again == true), right uses i + 1 instead of i = i + 1. A link to the 'rubber duck problem-solving' technique is provided: http://blog.codinghorror.com/rubber-duck-problem-solving/.
notes_text: This is a review duplicate of slide 43. The rubber duck debugging technique referenced is a well-known method where explaining your code line-by-line to an inanimate object (or anyone) helps find bugs.

title: The Loops That Keep On Giving - Bug Fixes (Review)
summary: Review slide showing corrected infinite loop bugs with fixes highlighted.
main_text: Same fixes highlighted as slide 44: while(again == true) fixes the assignment bug, and i = i + 1; fixes the missing update bug. Both corrections are highlighted in the code to draw attention to the changes.
notes_text: This is a review duplicate of slide 44. Always double-check loop conditions for = vs == and ensure every loop has a proper update statement.

title: Other Selection Structures - Section Header
summary: Section divider for additional selection structures: switch and ternary operator.
main_text: This is a section header slide introducing the Other Selection Structures section. The following slides cover the switch statement and the ternary (?) operator as alternatives to if-else chains.
notes_text: These are supplementary structures that students should be aware of but are not the primary focus of the course.

title: Switch Statement (Study on Own)
summary: Explains the switch statement syntax, constant cases, break requirement, fall-through behavior, and default case.
main_text: Again used to execute only certain blocks of code. Cases must be a constant. Best used to select an action when an expression could be 1 of a set of constant values. { ... } around entire set of cases and not individual case. Computer will execute code until a break statement is encountered, which allows multiple cases to be combined. Default statement is like an else statement. Syntax: switch(expr) // expr must eval to an int { case 0: // code executed when expr == 0; break; case 1: // code executed when expr == 1; break; case 2: case 3: case 4: // code executed when expr is 2, 3, or 4; break; default: // code executed when no other case is executed; break; }
notes_text: The switch statement is more readable than long if-else chains when comparing one expression against many constant values. The fall-through behavior (executing subsequent cases when break is missing) can be used intentionally to group cases but is a common source of bugs when unintentional.

title: Switch Statement - Missing Break Fall-Through
summary: Shows what happens when a break is forgotten in a switch: code falls through to subsequent cases until a break is found.
main_text: What if a break is forgotten? All code underneath will be executed until another break is encountered. Example: switch(expr) { case 0: // code executed when expr == 0; break; case 1: // code executed when expr == 1; // WHAT IF break was removed?; // break; case 2: case 3: case 4: // code executed when expr is 3, 4 or 5; break; default: // code executed when no other case is executed; break; }. If break is removed from case 1, then when expr is 1, the code for case 1 executes AND falls through to execute the code for cases 2/3/4 as well.
notes_text: Fall-through is one of the most common switch statement bugs. Some modern coding standards require a comment like '// fall-through' when intentional fall-through is used. C++17 added the [[fallthrough]] attribute for this purpose.

title: Ternary (?) Operator (Study on Own)
summary: Explains the ternary operator as a concise inline if-else expression: (condition) ? expr_if_true : expr_if_false.
main_text: A simple if..else statement can be expressed with the ? operator. Example: int x = (y > z) ? 2 : 1; is the same as: if(y > z) x = 2; else x = 1;. Syntax: (condition) ? expr_if_true : expr_if_false;. Meaning: the expression will result/return expr_if_true if condition evaluates to true or expr_if_false if condition evaluates to false. The ternary operator is useful for concise conditional assignments but should not be overused as it can reduce readability for complex conditions.
notes_text: The ternary operator is the only operator in C/C++ that takes three operands. It is commonly used for simple conditional assignments and in places where a full if-else statement would be syntactically awkward (e.g., inside cout statements or function arguments).

title: Loop Structures Additional Material - Section Header
summary: Section divider for additional loop structure material covering while loops, do..while, and more.
main_text: This is a section header slide introducing Loop Structures Additional Material. The following slides provide more detailed coverage of while loops, do..while loops, deriving loops from repetitive code, and flow charts for loop design.
notes_text: This additional material provides a deeper dive into loop structures, useful for students who want more practice and understanding of loop design.

title: Type 1: while Loops - Detailed
summary: Detailed explanation of while loops as repeating if statements, with numbered execution steps and a flowchart.
main_text: A while loop is essentially a repeating 'if' statement. The code shows: initialization (step 1), while(condition1) checked at steps 2, 5, 8 (T, T, F), body executes at steps 3 and 6 when condition is true, update at steps 4 and 7, then following statements at step 9 when condition is finally false. The flowchart shows: Initialization (i = 1) leads to Condition (i <= 1000) diamond, True branch goes to Loop task (cout << i << endl;) then Update Statement (i += 1) and back to Condition, False branch goes to Code after the loop.
notes_text: The while loop checks the condition before each iteration, so if the condition is initially false, the body never executes (zero iterations). This distinguishes it from the do..while loop.

images.description: Flowchart showing while loop structure with Initialization, Condition diamond, Loop task body, Update statement, and exit path

title: while vs. do..while Loops
summary: Compares while and do..while loops: while checks condition first (maybe 0 executions), do..while executes body first (at least 1 execution).
main_text: while loops have two variations: while and do..while. while: Cond is evaluated first. Body only executed if condition is true (maybe 0 times). Syntax: while(condition) { // code to be repeated // (should update condition) }. do..while: Body is executed at least once. Cond is evaluated after the body. Body is repeated if cond is true. Syntax: do { // code to be repeated // (should update condition) } while(condition);. Note the semicolon after the while condition in do..while.
notes_text: The key difference is guarantee of execution: while may execute 0 times, do..while always executes at least once. Choose based on whether you need to perform the action before checking the condition.

title: Deriving the Loop - From Repetitive Code to Loops
summary: Shows how to derive a loop from repetitive code by identifying the pattern in a guessing game with multiple guess attempts.
main_text: The left side shows repetitive code for a guessing game without loops: read a guess, check if correct, if not read another guess, check again, and so on with deeply nested if-else blocks. The code asks: 'What should we do here?' at the deepest nesting level. The right side shows a flowchart of the pattern: initialize secretNum, get first guess, check if correct, if not get another guess, repeat. The loop structure is identified: initialization, while(condition1) { body, update }. This process of identifying the repetitive pattern leads to: while(guess != secretNum) { cin >> guess; } which replaces all the nested if-else code.
notes_text: Deriving loops from repetitive patterns is a fundamental skill. The process involves: 1) write out the repetitive code, 2) identify what repeats, 3) identify what changes, 4) express the repetition as a loop with the changing part as the loop variable.

images.description: Flowchart showing the repetitive guess-check-guess pattern that naturally maps to a while loop structure

title: Using Flow Charts to Find Loops - do..while Pattern
summary: Shows how to use flowcharts to identify loop structures, demonstrating a do..while loop pattern for a guessing game.
main_text: Draw out a flow chart of the desired sequence and look for the repetitive sequence. Here we check at the end to see if we should repeat, which is perfect for a do..while loop. The flowchart shows: Accept Guess, check Correct (diamond), if False go to Accept Guess again (the dashed box indicates the do..while loop body), if True go to Post-Loop Code. The resulting code: do { accept_guess } while(!correct);. The repetitive block (Accept Guess + check Correct) forms the do..while body, with the condition checked after each execution.
notes_text: Flow charts are a powerful tool for designing loops. The position of the condition check in the flowchart determines which loop type is most natural: condition at the top suggests while, condition at the bottom suggests do..while.

images.description: Flowchart showing Accept Guess -> Correct? -> if False loop back, with dashed box identifying the do..while loop body

title: Finding the 'while' Structure
summary: Shows how to convert a do..while flowchart into a while loop by performing the first iteration before the loop.
main_text: The same guessing game flowchart is analyzed for a while loop structure. The do..while approach checks at the end: do { accept_guess } while(!correct);. But a while loop checks at the beginning of the loop, so we must accept one guess before starting: accept_guess; while(!correct) { accept_guess }. The right side shows the equivalent while loop flowchart: Accept Guess first, then loop: Not Correct? if True -> Accept Guess -> back to check, if False -> Post-Loop Code. This demonstrates that converting do..while to while requires duplicating the first iteration outside the loop.
notes_text: This slide illustrates the fundamental difference between while and do..while: the while version requires 'priming' the loop by executing the body once before entering the loop. This duplication is the tradeoff of using while when do..while is the natural fit.

images.description: Two flowcharts side by side: do..while (left) with condition at bottom, and while (right) with initial Accept Guess outside the loop and condition at top

title: Hand Tracing (1) - Two Loop Exercises
summary: Two hand-tracing exercises: trace a for loop from -n to n, and trace a sin function loop with step size t.
main_text: For the first program, trace through the code and show all changes to i for n = 2: int main() { int n; cin >> n; for(int i = -n; i <= n; i++) { cout << i << endl; } return 0; }. With n=2, i goes from -2 to 2 printing: -2, -1, 0, 1, 2. For the second program, trace through the code and show the output for t = PI/2, T = 2*PI: int main() { double t, T; cin >> t >> T; for(double th = 0; th < T; th += t) { cout << sin(th) << endl; } return 0; }. With t=PI/2 and T=2*PI, th takes values 0, PI/2, PI, 3*PI/2, printing sin values: 0, 1, 0, -1.
notes_text: Hand tracing is an essential debugging skill. For the second example, using floating-point values as loop variables can lead to precision issues. The number of iterations may vary slightly due to floating-point rounding.

title: Hand Tracing (2) - Two More Loop Exercises
summary: Two more hand-tracing exercises: a for loop with compound update (i=i+y), and a for loop with no init and decrementing second variable.
main_text: For the first program with x = 10, y = 2: int main() { int x, y; cin >> x >> y; for(int i=1; i <= x; i=i+y) { cout << i << endl; y++; } return 0; }. Here i starts at 1, step increases each iteration because y increments: i=1(y=2), i=3(y=3), i=6(y=4), then i=10 is not <= 10... actually i=1+2=3, 3+3=6, 6+4=10 but 10<=10 so prints 10, then i=10+5=15>10 exits. For the second program with x = 4, y = 11: for(; x < y; x++) { cout << x << " " << y << endl; y--; }. x increases, y decreases: prints 4 11, 5 10, 6 9, 7 8, then x=8 is not < y=7 so exits.
notes_text: These exercises test understanding of non-standard loop patterns: compound update expressions, variables modified inside the loop body, and the empty initialization in for loops. Students must trace carefully to get correct results.

title: bools, ints, and Conditions
summary: Explains that in C/C++, 0 means false and non-zero means true, and bool/int types can be used interchangeably in conditions.
main_text: Loops and conditional statements require a condition to be evaluated resulting in a true or false result. In C/C++: 0 means false / Non-Zero means true. bool type available in C++ uses 'true' and 'false' keywords but internally true = non-zero (usually 1) and false = 0. Any place a condition would be used, a bool or int type can be used and will be interpreted as bool. Examples: int x = 100; while(x) { x--; } loops until x reaches 0. bool done = false; while(!done) { cin >> done; } loops until user enters a non-zero value. int x=100, y=3, z=0; if(!x || (y && !z)) { /* code */ } evaluates !100 (false) || (3 (true) && !0 (true)) = false || true = true.
notes_text: The implicit conversion between int and bool is a C/C++ feature that can be both powerful and confusing. It enables idioms like while(x) but can also cause subtle bugs. Being explicit with comparisons (while(x != 0)) is often clearer.

title: Single Statement Bodies (Review)
summary: Review of single statement body rules for if/else/while/for constructs, recommending always using curly braces.
main_text: The Rule: Place code for an if, else if, or else construct in curly braces { ... }. The Exception: An if or else construct with a single statement body does not require { ... }. Another if counts as a single statement. However, you should ALWAYS prefer { ... } even in single statement bodies so that editing later does not introduce bugs. Same examples as slide 38 showing code without braces and the potential for misunderstanding which statements are inside which construct.
notes_text: This is a review duplicate of slide 38. The best practice recommendation to always use braces cannot be overstated.

title: Hand Tracing Solutions 1
summary: Provides solutions to the hand tracing exercises from slide 91: output for n=2 and sin function output for t=PI/2, T=2*PI.
main_text: First program solution with input n=2: for(int i = -n; i <= n; i++) produces output: -2, -1, 0, 1, 2. Second program solution with input t=PI/2 and T=2*PI: for(double th = 0; th < T; th += t) with cout << sin(th), th takes values 0, PI/2, PI, 3*PI/2, producing output: 0, 1, 0, -1.
notes_text: These solutions confirm the expected output from hand tracing. For the second program, note that sin(0)=0, sin(PI/2)=1, sin(PI)=0, sin(3*PI/2)=-1. The value th=2*PI is not included because the condition is th < T (strict less than).

title: Hand Tracing Solutions 2
summary: Provides solutions to the hand tracing exercises from slide 92: outputs for compound update loop and converging variables loop.
main_text: First program solution with input x=10, y=2: for(int i=1; i <= x; i=i+y) with y++ inside body. Trace: i=1(print 1, y becomes 3), i=1+2=3 but wait y was 2 at first increment so i=3(print... let me recalculate). Actually: i=1,y=2: print 1, y++=3. i=1+2=3,y=3: print 3... Hmm. Looking at the solution output: 1, 4, 8. So: i=1(y=2, print 1, y=3), i=1+3=4(y=3, print 4, y=4), i=4+4=8(y=4, print 8, y=5), i=8+5=13>10 exit. Second program solution with input x=4, y=11: for(; x < y; x++) with y-- inside body. Output: 4 11, 5 10, 6 9, 7 8. Then x=8, y=7, 8 < 7 is false, exit.
notes_text: The first solution is tricky because the update expression i=i+y uses the value of y from AFTER y++ in the body. The for loop update happens after the body executes, so y has already been incremented. This is a subtle sequencing issue.

title: Array and Function Details - Section Header
summary: Section divider for detailed coverage of arrays and functions in the review portion.
main_text: This is a section header slide introducing Array and Function Details. The following slides provide more detailed coverage of array operations, function prototypes, and related topics.
notes_text: This section provides a more comprehensive review of array and function concepts, including topics like accessing elements, initialization, bounds checking, and function prototypes.

title: Function Prototypes - Detailed
summary: Explains why function prototypes are needed: the compiler scans top-to-bottom and needs to see a prototype or definition before any call.
main_text: The compiler (g++/clang++) needs to see a function's prototype or definition before it allows a call to that function. The compiler will scan a file from top to bottom. If it encounters a call to a function before the actual function definition it will complain with a Compile error. Unless a prototype ('declaration') for the function is provided earlier. A prototype only needs to include data types for the parameters but not their names (ends with ';'). Prototype is used to check that you are calling it with the correct syntax (i.e. parameter data types and return type) like a menu at a restaurant. Example without prototype: main() calls triangle_area(5.0,3.5) but definition is below - compiler error. Example with prototype: double triangle_area(double, double); before main(), compiler sees it and expects the definition later.
notes_text: Prototypes are essential for code organization. They allow you to put main() at the top of the file (which is conventional) while defining helper functions below. They also enable separate compilation where functions are defined in different files.

title: The Need For Prototypes - Mutual Recursion
summary: Shows why prototypes are necessary: mutually recursive functions (f1 calls f2, f2 calls f1) cannot be ordered without prototypes.
main_text: You might say: 'I don't like prototypes. I'll define each function before I call it.' How would you order the functions in the program on the left if you did NOT want to use prototypes? You can't! Left side shows: int f1(int x) { return f2(x-1); } int f2(int y) { if(y <= 0) return 1; else return f1(y); } int main() { cout << f1(5) << endl; }. f1 calls f2 and f2 calls f1 - no matter which order you put them in, one will be called before it is defined. Right side shows the solution with prototypes: int f1(int x); int f2(int y); at the top, then main, then the function definitions. Prototypes break the circular dependency.
notes_text: Mutual recursion is the definitive case for why prototypes exist. Even without mutual recursion, prototypes allow cleaner code organization and are required for separate compilation across multiple files.

title: Overloading: A Function's Signature (Review)
summary: Review of function overloading: signature uniqueness determined by name and parameter types, not return type.
main_text: What makes up a function signature unique: the name, and the number and type of arguments. No two functions are allowed to have the same signature. The following 6 functions are unique and allowed to have different implementations: int f1(int), int f1(double), int f1(int, double), void f1(char), double f1(), int f1(int, char). Return type does not make a function unique: int f1() and double f1() are not unique and thus not allowable. Two functions with the same name are said to be 'overloaded': int max(int, int); double max(double, double);.
notes_text: This is a review duplicate of slide 19. Function overloading is a key C++ feature that supports polymorphism and code reuse.

title: Accessing An Element
summary: Explains how to access individual array elements using any expression as an index, with examples showing constants, variables, and function calls as indices.
main_text: Once an array is declared, there is nothing 'special' about it. Each variable must be initialized and accessed 1 at a time. To access an individual variable/element of an array of size n, use the name of the array followed by square brackets containing ANY expression (constant, variable, arithmetic) that will evaluate to an index from 0 to n-1. Note: Indexing starts at 0. Example: int x = 1, myval = 5; int scores[10]; scores[4] = 73; scores[x] = 82 (sets scores[1]); scores[2*x + 1] = 93 (sets scores[3]); scores[1+max(x,myval)] = 88 (sets scores[6]). The key is you can generate the index of the desired element using any legal C++ code that will result in the desired index. Memory diagram shows scores at addresses 520-544 with indices [0]-[6], values: ??, 82, ??, 93, 73, ??, 88.
notes_text: The flexibility of using any expression as an array index is what makes arrays powerful. Combined with loop variables, this allows systematic processing of all elements.

title: Initializing Arrays With Constants
summary: Shows how to initialize arrays using initialization lists with constants, including size inference and partial initialization.
main_text: Arrays can be initialized with constants when they are declared. To do so, use an initialization list which is a comma separated list of constants in {}. Exception to the minimalist C/C++ rule: If fewer values are provided than the size of the array, remaining elements will be filled with 0s. If an initialization list is provided you need not specify the size in the square brackets (i.e. just use empty []) as the compiler can figure out what size the array must be by counting the initial values. Examples: int data[5] = {9, 7, 8, 9, 5} allocates 5 ints with given values. double dec[4] = {0.25, 0.3} allocates 4 doubles: 0.25, 0.3, 0, 0. char str1[3] = {'C', 'S', '\0'} or equivalently char str2[3] = "CS". int data[] = {9, 7, 8, 9, 5} allocates array of size 5. double dec[] = {0.25, 0.3, 0.18, 0.2} allocates array of size 4. char str2[] = "CS" allocates array of size 3.
notes_text: The initialization list syntax is the most common way to create small arrays with known values. The zero-fill behavior for partial initialization is guaranteed by the C/C++ standard and is very useful for initializing arrays to all zeros: int arr[100] = {0};.

title: Loops and Arrays (1)
summary: Demonstrates the power of combining loops with arrays: using the loop variable as the array index for initialization and input.
main_text: The real power of arrays is found when you combine them with loops. Use the loop control variable (int i) to serve as the index of the array entry to be modified or accessed. Whether the array has 1 or 1,000,000 elements, our code size does not grow. Example: int x = 1, myval = 5; int scores[100]; // Initialize all to 0: for(int i=0; i < 100; i++) { scores[i] = 0; }. Or read in all entries: for(int i=0; i < 100; i++) { cin >> scores[i]; }. Memory diagram shows scores array with all values set to 0 at addresses 520-540.
notes_text: This is the fundamental pattern: use the loop variable i as the array index. This pattern scales to any array size without changing the code structure, only the loop bound.

title: Index vs. Value (Review)
summary: Review of the distinction between array index and value, showing that any expression can be used as an index.
main_text: The expression in the square brackets is an index. Using array[index] yields the data/value in the array at that index. An index can be ANY EXPRESSION, even the value from an array or the return value from a function. For an array declared to be size n, only indices 0 to n-1 are legal. Same example as slide 9 with scores containing {9, 0, 7, 8, 6}: scores[2*i+1] with i=1 yields scores[3]=8, scores[scores[1]] yields scores[0]=9, scores[max(4,2)] yields scores[4]=6. Labeled with 'x=_', 'y=_', 'z=_' for students to fill in.
notes_text: This is a review duplicate of slide 9. The index-value distinction is fundamental and worth reviewing multiple times.

title: Important C/C++ Rule: Array Size
summary: Reiterates that C/C++ array sizes must be compile-time constants, and for this course, over-allocating with a large max size is acceptable.
main_text: C/C++ needs to know the SIZE of the array when the program is compiled, not when it is run. This implies the size of the array must be ONE, FIXED (or constant) size every time the program is run. GOOD: int data[24]; where 24 is known at compile time. BAD: int n; cin >> n; int data[n]; where n is not known at compile time. For this course, we will just allocate a LARGE array of the maximum size potentially needed and then use only a portion of it as the program runs. Future courses will teach you how to deal with this correctly and not waste array space. Example: int data[100]; int n; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; }.
notes_text: This is a review/elaboration of slides 10-11. The over-allocation approach is simple and works for introductory coursework. Professional code uses dynamic allocation (new/delete) or standard library containers (std::vector) instead.

title: A Common Error - Out of Bounds Array Access
summary: Warns about out-of-bounds array access causing data corruption or segmentation faults, and shows how to validate indices.
main_text: Care must be taken to ensure no index is used that will lead to an out-of-bounds access. Such an access will either corrupt other data or cause the program to crash! These are often known as segmentation faults. When you see one, your first thought should be to check for a bad array index! Example bugs: int scores[20]; for(i=0; i <= 20; i++) { scores[i] = 0; } - the <= 20 should be < 20, because valid indices are 0-19, and scores[20] is out of bounds. cin >> i; scores[i] = 100; - unsafe because i could be any value. Safe version: if(i >= 0 && i < 20) { scores[i] = 100; }. Memory diagram shows scores array with indices [0]-[19] and a question mark at position [20].
notes_text: Off-by-one errors in array bounds are one of the most common bugs in C/C++. The pattern for(i=0; i < size; i++) is correct, while for(i=0; i <= size; i++) accesses one element past the end. Always validate user-provided indices before using them.

title: Exercise Solution - Range Check Conditions
summary: Solution to the range check exercise: option b (-1 <= x <= 5) is NOT a valid C/C++ condition for checking range [-1 to 5].
main_text: Which of the following is NOT a condition to check if the integer x is in the range [-1 to 5]? a. x >= -1 && x <= 5 - VALID: standard AND-based range check. b. -1 <= x <= 5 - INVALID (highlighted in red): this is chained comparison syntax that does not work as intended in C/C++. It evaluates left-to-right: (-1 <= x) produces 0 or 1, then (0_or_1 <= 5) is always true. c. !(x < -1 || x > 5) - VALID: DeMorgan's equivalent of option a. d. x > -2 && x < 6 - VALID: equivalent range for integers (since x is int, x > -2 means x >= -1, and x < 6 means x <= 5). The answer is b.
notes_text: This exercise tests understanding of C/C++ comparison syntax. The chained comparison in option b is valid Python syntax but not valid C/C++ logic. Students must remember to always compare two values at a time using explicit logical operators.
